title: Sitting and holding a pencil
keyIdea: Good writing starts before the pencil moves: feet flat, sit tall, and the other hand holds the paper. Pinch the pencil gently with thumb and pointer finger on the paint just above the wood, resting it on the middle finger. Most letters start at the top; e starts in the middle.

kid: Before you write, get ready. Put your feet flat on the floor. Sit up tall. Your other hand holds the paper still.
Pinch the pencil with your thumb and your pointer finger. Let it rest on your middle finger. Hold it on the paint, just above the wood.
Hold the pencil gently, like a baby bird. Do not squeeze it hard. A tight fist makes a wobbly line.
Most letters start at the top. Put your pencil at the top of c, l, n and o. The letter e is different. It starts in the middle.
adult: The English national curriculum expects Year 1 children to sit correctly at a table, hold a pencil comfortably and correctly, and begin to form lower-case letters in the right direction, starting and finishing in the right place. Posture and grip come first because a stable body frees the hand and fingers for small, controlled movements.

A good set-up: feet flat on the floor (a box or footstool works if they dangle), hips back in the chair, table about elbow height, and the non-writing hand holding the paper. The usual grip is the tripod: pencil pinched between thumb and index finger, resting on the side of the middle finger, about 2 cm from the tip. A four-finger version is also fine if it is comfortable; studies find it is just as fast and readable.

Common mistakes: a fist grip, where the whole arm does the moving; holding right on the wooden tip, which hides the line and smudges; holding near the top, which makes the pencil wobble; squeezing so hard that the hand tires and the paper tears; swinging feet or slumping; and starting letters at the bottom. Left-handed children are best holding a little further up and tilting the paper to the right so they can see what they write.

Keep practice short and playful. Short or chunky pencils, crayons broken in half and pegs on a line build the pinch. Say the start out loud: "top, and down". Praise the start and direction more than neatness. If holding a pencil still hurts or stays very awkward after a term at school, mention it to the teacher.

familyTip: Snap a crayon in half so only a small piece is left. It is hard to hold a tiny crayon in a fist, so little fingers find the pinch on their own. Draw big circles together, starting at the top.

practice.prompt: Where do your feet go when you write?
practice.hint: Think of Pip in the lab. What made Pip steady?
practice.explain: Feet go flat on the floor, or on a box if they do not reach. Then your body stays still.

practice.prompt: Sam has {n} pencils. Where should Sam hold each one?
choices: on the paint, just above the wood
practice.hint: Remember the giant pencil in the lab. Which spot made a smooth line?
practice.explain: All {n} pencils are held the same way: on the paint, just above the wood. Then you can see your line.

practice.prompt: Each hand has 5 fingers. You pinch with 2 fingers and rest the pencil on 1 more. How many fingers hold the pencil?
practice.hint: Count the pinch fingers, then add the one the pencil rests on.
practice.explain: Thumb and pointer finger pinch, and the middle finger is the rest: 3 fingers.

practice.prompt: Ava writes {n} letter l's. Where does each l start?
practice.hint: Tap the dots again in the lab. Where did the pencil go first?
practice.explain: Every l starts at the top and goes straight down, all {n} times.

pool.prompt: What does your other hand do when you write?
pool.hint: If the paper slides, the line goes wrong. What can stop it?
pool.explain: The other hand holds the paper still, so it does not slide away.

pool.prompt: Which grip helps you draw a smooth line?
choices: a pinch with thumb and pointer finger
pool.hint: Look back at the three lines you drew. Which one was smooth?
pool.explain: The pinch lets your fingers make small moves. A fist moves the whole arm, so the line wobbles.

pool.prompt: How tight should you hold your pencil?
pool.hint: Think of holding a baby bird. Not too hard, not too soft.
pool.explain: Hold it gently. Squeezing makes your hand tired. Too loose and it falls.

pool.prompt: Where does the letter e start?
pool.hint: e was the different one in the lab. Where was its start dot?
pool.explain: e starts in the middle, goes across, then round. Most other letters start at the top.

pool.prompt: Why is holding right on the wooden tip a problem?
pool.hint: If your fingers are at the very end, what can you not see?
pool.explain: Fingers on the tip cover what you write and get messy. Hold on the paint, just above the wood.

pool.prompt: Your feet do not reach the floor. What can help?
choices: put a box under your feet
pool.hint: Feet need something flat to rest on. What could you put there?
pool.explain: A box or a stool under your feet works like the floor. Now you are steady.

pool.prompt: Leo writes {n} letter c's. Where does each c start?
pool.hint: c is a round letter. Where did the pencil start in the lab?
pool.explain: Each c starts at the top and curls round to the left, all {n} times.

pool.prompt: Mia gets ready to write {n} times. Each time she checks 3 things: feet, back, other hand. How many checks is that?
pool.hint: She does 3 checks each time. Count in threes, {n} times.

pool.prompt: How should you sit when you write?
pool.hint: Think of Pip after you fixed the back. How did Pip look?
pool.explain: Sit tall. Then you can see the paper and your arm can move.

visual.caption: Ready to write or not yet? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: get Pip ready to write, find the best spot on a giant pencil, draw with three grips, and tap where letters start.
